graphicEarnsIt.says: An audio waveform: a row of grey bars of varying height reading as loudness over time, with six of them raised and turned lime. Those spikes read as the accented beats in the track, and the caption pins them to the film's cuts. So the picture encodes WHERE in the audio the cuts land, which is the timing claim the words only assert. LEFT shows nothing at all; every one of its six frames is type on a gradient.

An audio waveform: grey bars are the amplitude of a track over time, and the tall lime spikes standing above them are the beat onsets, so the picture shows WHERE in the sound the hits fall and, with the caption, claims each cut is placed on one of them. It encodes timing and rhythm, a quantity the words 'on the beat' only assert. LEFT has nothing but a glow, which is decoration.

An audio waveform over time: a row of grey amplitude bars with a handful of tall lime spikes standing above them, labelled beat.wav on one end and 'every cut on a beat' on the other. It reads as the soundtrack's envelope with the cut points marked on it, so the eye can see that the edit lands on the loud transients rather than being told so. The spacing of the lime spikes is the rhythm itself, and it is uneven in the way real music is, which is what makes it read as a measurement instead of an ornament. LEFT has no picture anywhere in the six beats.

perBeat.why: Identical frames: one huge lime word on the blue glow, single focal point, nothing separates the two cuts.
Same white THEM at the same size and weight; contrast is strong on both and no difference is visible.
Both put the black-on-lime STOP slab dead centre with equal margins; the deliberate centring reads the same on each.
SCROLLING runs edge to edge on both and touches the frame margins identically, so both share the same tightness.

It is the word-on-empty-space slide, and it is the beat that most needed proof.
